title: A container literal stores its elements without the widening the position declares.
text: [`lower::Lowering::lower_array_literal`] lowers every element with no expected type and stores whatever it gets, so `array<float> $p = [4, 2.5];` writes the integer `4`'s *bits* into a slot the `float` read then reinterprets — `4.9406564584125E-324` instead of `4`. `rule:types/implicit-widening` names that widening as the one conversion the language performs on its own, and [`lower::Lowering::coerce`] is where it is performed everywhere else: `$p[] = $n` and `$p["k"] = $n` are already right, which is why only the literal is wrong. The element type exists in the checker — `nvs_types::expr::literals`'s `check_array_literal` checks each element against it — and nothing records it, so closing this half is an `nvs_types::expr_table::ExprInfo` row plus one `coerce` per element. An **object literal** shows the same symptom from a different cause: `check_object_literal` infers each field against no expectation, so `{rate: 5}` at a `{rate: float}` is decided by shape assignability and the per-field conversion belongs to that boundary rather than to the literal — a representation question, and the reason this is recorded rather than fixed where it was found. `docs/examples/lang/types/widening-without-as/03-a-price-list-that-mixes-both.nvs` is the proof that carries it.
